books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Taft, Roosevelt, and the Election of 1912
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Table of 1912 election results; figures from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9 (rounded).
stimulus.text:
| Candidate | Party | Popular vote | Electoral votes |
| Woodrow Wilson | Democratic | 42% | 435 |
| Theodore Roosevelt | Progressive ('Bull Moose') | 27% | 88 |
| William Howard Taft | Republican | 23% | 8 |
| Eugene V. Debs | Socialist | 6% | 0 |

Percentages rounded. Source: 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9.

stem: The table best supports the conclusion that the Republican split

options.text: helped Taft win reelection to the presidency
options.misconception: Taft finished third with 23 percent and 8 electoral votes; the split destroyed his campaign, it did not help it.

options.text: handed Wilson the election by splitting the Republican vote
had no effect on the outcome of the election
options.misconception: Roosevelt and Taft together won 50 percent of the vote; united, they would have beaten Wilson's 42 percent.

options.text: elected Eugene Debs of the Socialist Party
options.misconception: Debs won 6 percent and no electoral votes; the Socialist candidate did not win.

rationales.A: Taft finished third with 8 electoral votes. The split ended his presidency; it did not save it.
rationales.B: Roosevelt's 27 percent and Taft's 23 percent add to 50 percent, more than Wilson's 42. Divided, the two Republicans lost; the table shows the split itself decided the election.
rationales.C: The split mattered decisively. Together the two Republicans won half the popular vote, more than Wilson's 42 percent.
rationales.D: Debs won 6 percent and no electoral votes. The split elected Wilson, not Debs.
rationales.general:
1. Add the Republican pieces. Roosevelt's 27 percent plus Taft's 23 percent equals 50 percent, more than Wilson's 42.
2. Read the electoral result. Wilson took 435 electoral votes while the two Republicans split the rest.
3. Name the cause. The division, not Wilson's popularity, decided the election.
Remember: when two candidates fish in the same pond, add their shares before judging who really won the argument.
